newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: NZ dollar ends US1c lower after RBNZ statement.
newsitem.headline: NZ dollar ends US1c lower after RBNZ statement.

text.p: The New Zealand dollar ended one cent weaker against the U.S. dollar on Thursday after the Reserve Bank said monetary conditions were tighter than necessary.
After opening at US$0.7096/03 the Kiwi traded down to 0.6975 before finding a support level and closing at 0.7006/13. On the Trade Weighted Index it closed at 66.92 from an opening of 67.73.
"Straight after those comments we saw very large selling in the currency as you would expect, predominantly from offshore but we saw some local clients selling as well," a chief dealer said.

"For the first half cent in the Kiwi there was not a great deal of liquidity. We found buying interest around 0.7050 initially then down towards 0.7030 but there has been pretty heavy selling all day. We didn't find any serious buying until we got below US70c -- down towards 69 and three quarters in fact."
He said some offshore traders will be caught unawares by a dollar 100 points lower than where they left it.
"I think around 0.6975 it has found a little bit of a base and I wouldn't be surprised to see it edge back towards 0.7025/35 overnight.

"The RBNZ have sent a signal to the market that even with interest rates going down as they have over the last few weeks, the strength of the currency has more than offset that and monetary conditions have firmed more than they considered necessary."
Meanwhile, analysts said foreign investors' appetite for New Zealand assets was unlikely to be dimmed by the statement.
While the pace of eurokiwi and samurai bond issuance might ease up, yields even at new lower levels were still too tempting for offshore investors to resist, they said.

"New Zealand interest rates, even at nine percent, are still relatively high compared with those in Japan and Europe, although the pace of issues may slow in coming weeks," Macquarie Bank economist Joanne Gudgin told Reuters Financial Television.

"If the short-term interest rates remain above nine percent, I expect good support for the Kiwi around the US69.75 cent level," Oliver Kam, assistant director of Standard Chartered Asia in Hong Kong, told RFTV.
Graham Bibby, managing director of Richmond Asset Management in Hong Kong, said the market had over-reacted to the bank's statement and should find solid support around US69.70 cents.
"As long as that support level holds, I think foreign investors will be moving back into the Kiwi," he said.
